record.paper_title: A survey of open questions in adaptive therapy: bridging mathematics and clinical translation
record.original_question: Is real-time patient-specific prediction feasible for adaptive therapy, and what monitoring, model calibration, validation, sensitivity analysis, identifiability analysis, and biomarker quality are required before predictions should guide dose modulation? Given a clinical marker such as prostate-specific antigen, circulating tumor DNA, circulating tumor cells, urine markers, imaging, or another disease-specific biomarker, when can a mathematical model accurately describe patient-specific dynamics well enough to predict subsequent response, and when should it be rejected because it cannot describe the data?

evidence.quote: Predicting precisely when a patient will progress during adaptive therapy offers the opportunity to appropriately modulate treatment, thereby extending patient response and survival.
This requires sufficient monitoring of an individual patient’s disease using appropriate clinical markers.
Prior to making model predictions, the chosen model should be calibrated and validated to demonstrate that it can accurately describe patient-specific biomarker dynamics [111].
If the model cannot accurately describe the data, then it should not be used to make predictions of subsequent patient responses.
Model-predictions are dependent on the quality and time-resolution of patient-specific biomarkers.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a patient undergoing adaptive cancer therapy, in which the dose or scheduling of treatment is dynamically modulated in response to longitudinal measurements of a disease-specific biomarker (for example, prostate-specific antigen, circulating tumor DNA, circulating tumor cell counts, urine markers, or quantitative imaging). Let y(t) denote the time series of such a biomarker, and suppose one wishes to use a mathematical model M (with parameter vector θ ∈ Θ ⊂ ℝ^p) of tumor–treatment dynamics to forecast the patient's future biomarker trajectory and, in particular, the time of disease progression, in real time.

Formulate and resolve the following questions:

(a) Identify general necessary conditions on the sampling frequency and noise level of y(t), on the structural and practical identifiability of θ given the observation map, on calibration and validation protocols (e.g., out-of-sample prediction error, sensitivity analysis of forecasts to θ), and on the quality of the biomarker as a surrogate for tumor burden, under which patient-specific real-time prediction of progression times is feasible with quantifiable uncertainty suitable to guide dose modulation.

(b) Provide a decision rule (a goodness-of-fit / model-adequacy criterion) that, given the calibration data of a single patient, determines when the model M may legitimately be used to issue forecasts, and when M must be rejected as unable to describe that patient's dynamics.

(c) For at least one concrete choice of biomarker and corresponding mechanistic model, demonstrate prospectively (not merely retrospectively) that the resulting predictions are sufficiently accurate and calibrated to inform clinical dose modulation.
artifact.status_search_result: The feasibility of real-time, patient-specific prediction for adaptive cancer therapy remains an active open research question. Recent works on PSA-based prostate cancer adaptive therapy and ctDNA-informed models report progress on retrospective calibration and identifiability, but prospective clinical validation enabling forecast-driven dose modulation has not been established. No definitive solution is reported in the literature.

status_evidence.snippet: Is real-time patient prediction feasible? ... the chosen model should be calibrated and validated to demonstrate that it can accurately describe patient-specific biomarker dynamics.
status_evidence.claim: The question is explicitly listed among open questions in the field.

status_evidence.title: Forecasting individual patient response to treatment with adaptive therapy (Brady-Nicholls et al.)
status_evidence.snippet: Patient-specific calibration of a simple mathematical model of prostate cancer using PSA dynamics retrospectively predicts response to intermittent therapy.
status_evidence.claim: Retrospective patient-specific forecasting has been demonstrated for PSA, but prospective real-time forecasting guiding dose modulation has not been clinically validated.
